steps.title: What this step is for
steps.text:
One molecule crossing the confocal spot does not always leave one burst. It dims for a few hundred microseconds — to the edge of the volume and back, an acceptor blink — and the burst search, which sees only a count rate, ends one burst and starts another. Downstream, each fragment counts as its own molecule.

This tool merges the fragments back together and writes a new burst folder. The folder you start from is never modified, so a threshold can be tried, looked at, and thrown away.

You do not need your own data to follow this. Press 🧪 Load demo in the toolbar: it simulates a measurement in which 300 molecules crossed the focus and about 60 % of those crossings were interrupted, then runs the ordinary burst search over it. Everything below is checked against that known 300.

await.hint: Press 🧪 Load demo. The first time it simulates the photon stream and searches it for bursts, which takes a few seconds; afterwards it is instant.

steps.title: Step 1 — the damage, in one number
steps.text:
The status block now says what the demo contains and what the search made of it: 300 molecules → about 430 bursts.

Those 130 extra bursts are not molecules. They are second and third pieces of crossings the search cut up, and every one of them carries fewer photons than the crossing did — which is exactly the noise fusion is here to undo.

(With your own data you will not know the 300. That is what the rest of this tour is for: the burst count alone cannot tell you whether you have fused too little or too much, so we will look at the evidence instead.)

steps.title: Step 2 — see the evidence before choosing anything
steps.text:
Press Run (the green ▶). Nothing is written: it reads the burst tables and estimates P(same molecule) against the lag between bursts — the probability that a burst arriving τ after another one is the same molecule recurring rather than a different one arriving by chance.

Look at the first plot. It rises to about 0.9 at short lags and falls away by a few tens of milliseconds. That hump is the split crossings: pairs of bursts a millisecond apart are far commoner than random arrivals would explain.

steps.title: Step 3 — read your threshold off that curve
steps.text:
The dashed line is this number; the dotted line is the longest lag that still meets it — the gap that will actually be fused.

Walk it. Type 0.9 and Run: about 340 bursts — conservative, some splits left unrepaired. Then 0.7: about 300, which is the truth. Then 0.5: about 283, now below the truth, because at this burst rate some genuinely different molecules also land within the window.

That is the whole trade-off, and it is why the curve is on screen rather than a number. On your own data you will not have the 300 — you will have the summary table, which is the next step.

steps.title: Step 4 — the ceiling that is not about probability
steps.text:
Now look at where the dotted line sits. On a dilute sample the curve stays above any sensible threshold out to tens of milliseconds — the molecule really is the same one, because there is hardly anyone else in the sample.

Fusing on that would be right about the molecule and ruinous for the burst. A burst on disk is one (first photon, last photon) interval, so bridging a 70 ms gap puts 70 ms of background inside the burst.

This box stops that. The probability answers “same molecule?”; this answers “at what cost?”. Leave it at 10 ms unless you know why not — on the demo the gaps are under 3 ms, so it never binds.

steps.title: Step 5 — judge it from the table, not the burst count
steps.text:
Set the threshold back to 0.7, Run, and read the summary. These are the rows that decide it:

• Proximity ratio (std) — should fall (on the demo: 0.041 → 0.033). The demo has one FRET population, so its whole width is shot noise; putting the fragments back together removes some of it. This is the row that says fusion helped.
• Proximity ratio (mean) — should barely move. If it walks, you are merging populations, not fragments.
• Photons per burst — rises, and the photon histogram loses weight from its short tail. The tail was the fragments.
• Duration (mean) — rises modestly. Orders of magnitude means the ceiling is too generous.

steps.title: Step 6 — write the fused folder
steps.text:
Press Save (the 💾).

This is the slow half: the photon streams are reopened and every column is re-derived over the real span, so the result is an ordinary burst folder — BVA, 2CDE, the MLE, H2MM and the browser read it with no idea that fusion happened.

The plots then switch from the preview to what was actually written (the legend says which). The two differ by the photons the bridged gaps brought in, and the fu4 companion records that number for every burst — worth a look before you build on the folder.

steps.title: Step 7 — and then carry on down the pipeline
steps.text:
In the Burst Analysis window the later steps now point at the fused folder; running the burst search again supersedes that and takes you back.

One thing to know: results already computed on the original folder — BVA, 2CDE, per-burst MLE lifetimes — are not carried over. They have one row per original burst and a burst folder is merged by position, so they would line up one burst's lifetime against another's efficiency. Recompute them here, which is exactly why fusion sits before them.

Your own data goes in the same box the demo used.
